'''Himuro Gongen''' (氷室権現) is a syncretic deity of Shinto and Buddhism, enshrined in various places across Japan in connection with {{ill|Ice house (building)|en|Ice house (building)|qid=Q253893|lt=ice houses}} known as Himuro in Japan, which are facilities for storing natural ice. The term "Gongen" (権現) refers to a Buddha appearing in the temporary form of a Shinto deity, and Himuro Gongen is deeply associated with the faith concerning the preservation and use of ice.

The {{ill|Himuro Shrine|en|Himuro Shrine|qid=Q11549570|lt=Himuro Shrine}} in {{ill|Kasugano, Nara City|ja|春日野町|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasugano, Nara|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q18988212}}, Nara City, Nara Prefecture, was established after the relocation of the capital to Heian-kyō to enshrine the himuro of Nara and is also known as Himuro Gongen.<ref>https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%B0%B7%E5%AE%A4</ref>

This shrine has been worshiped as a deity overseeing the preservation and supply of ice.

Additionally, at the summit of {{ill|Mount Himuro|ja|氷室岳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Himuro|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11549563}} (elevation 562.6 meters), located on the border between {{ill|Yanai, Yamaguchi|en|Yanai, Yamaguchi|qid=Q819678|lt=Yanai, Yamaguchi}} and {{ill|Iwakuni|en|Iwakuni|qid=Q329797|lt=Iwakuni, Yamaguchi}} in Yamaguchi Prefecture, there is a small shrine dedicated to Himuro Gongen.<ref>https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%B0%B7%E5%AE%A4%E5%B2%B3</ref>

This mountain has long been an object of mountain worship and is locally known as "Suō Fuji" (周防富士) or "Dakeyama" (嶽山).

Furthermore, within the grounds of {{ill|Son'ei-ji Temple|ja|法多山尊永寺|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hattasan Soneiji|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11555090}} in {{ill|Fukuroi, Shizuoka|en|Fukuroi, Shizuoka|qid=Q821337|lt=Fukuroi, Shizuoka}}, Shizuoka Prefecture, there is another Himuro Shrine, which has been worshiped since ancient times as a deity for healing illnesses.<ref>https://www.hattasan.or.jp/annai/12himurojinja/</ref>

At this shrine, the "Kenpyō-shiki" (献氷式, Ice Offering Ceremony) is held annually on July 1st, where ice is dedicated to pray for relief from the summer heat and for good health.

The faith in Himuro Gongen originates from a time when ice preservation technology was highly valuable, and people revered the blessings of ice as sacred, offering gratitude and prayers. Even today, this tradition continues through various Himuro Shrines and related festivals across Japan.

== Himuro in Japan ==

In Japan, during times when there was no technology for {{ill|Icemaker|en|Icemaker|qid=Q4271166|lt=artificial ice production}} from spring to autumn, it was necessary to store natural ice formed in winter to prevent it from melting. Although there are no precise records, it is believed that caves or holes dug in the ground were covered with huts made of {{ill|Thatching|en|Thatching|qid=Q874531|lt=thatch}} and other materials to keep the ice cool. The inside of the Himuro remained cooler than the outside air due to the {{ill|Enthalpy of vaporization|ja|気化熱|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/evaporative cooling|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 蒸発熱|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q483538}} of {{ill|Groundwater|en|Groundwater|qid=Q161598|lt=groundwater}}, allowing ice to be preserved until summer, especially in cool mountain areas. In such times, when only natural ice could be stored, summer ice was a precious commodity, long reserved for the {{ill|Royal court|en|Royal court|qid=Q1134237|lt=Imperial Court}} and the {{ill|shogun family|ja|将軍家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/shogunate|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11458630}}.

Historically, the first recorded mention appears in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|en|Nihon Shoki|qid=Q813935|lt=Nihon Shoki}}, in the 62nd year of {{ill|Emperor Nintoku|en|Emperor Nintoku|qid=Q313119|lt=Emperor Nintoku}}’s reign, describing how {{ill|Nukata no Ónakachuhiko no Miko|ja|額田大中彦皇子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nukata no Ōnakatsuhiko|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q55177820}} discovered something shining while hunting in {{ill|Tsuge|ja|闘鶏国造}} (modern-day {{ill|fukusumichou|ja|福住町|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fukuzumi, Tenri City|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q16767272}}, {{ill|Nara Prefecture|en|Nara Prefecture|qid=Q131287|lt=Nara Prefecture}}). {{ill|Mokkan|en|Mokkan|qid=Q4299994|lt=Wooden tablets}} excavated from the site of {{ill|Prince Nagaya|en|Prince Nagaya|qid=Q1963492|lt=Prince Nagaya}}’s residence from the {{ill|Nara period|af|Nara-tydperk|ar|فترة نارا|bcl|Panahon nin Nara|bg|Нара (период)|bn|নারা যুগ|ca|Període Nara|ckb|سەردەمی نارا|cs|Období Nara|de|Nara-Zeit|el|Περίοδος Νάρα|eo|Epoko de Nara|es|Período Nara|eu|Nara aroa|fa|دوره نارا|fi|Nara-kausi|fr|Époque de Nara|gl|Período Nara|he|תקופת נארה|hr|Nara (razdoblje)|hu|Nara-kor|id|Zaman Nara|it|Periodo Nara|ja|奈良時代|jv|Periodhe Nara|ko|나라 시대|lt|Nara laikotarpis|ml|നാറ കാലഘട്ടം|ms|Zaman Nara|nl|Naraperiode|nn|Naratida|no|Nara-perioden|oc|Periòde de Nara|pl|Nara (okres)|ps|نارا|pt|Período Nara|ro|Perioada Nara|ru|Период Нара|sh|Nara period|simple|Nara period|sk|Obdobie Nara|sl|Obdobje Nara|sr|Нара период|sv|Naraperioden|th|ยุคนาระ|tl|Panahong Nara|tok|tenpo pi kulupu lawa Nala|tr|Nara Dönemi|uk|Період Нара|ur|نارا دور|vi|Thời kỳ Nara|war|Panahon Nara|wuu|奈良时代|zh|奈良時代|zh_min_nan|Nara sî-tāi|zh_yue|奈良時代|qid=Q189178|lt=Nara period}} also bear the inscription "Tsuge Himuro" (都祁氷室).<ref group="note">Excavated in {{ill|Nara|ja|奈良}}.</ref>

In the Nihon Shoki, during the chronicle of {{ill|Emperor Kōtoku|en|Emperor Kōtoku|qid=Q317980|lt=Emperor Kōtoku}}, the surname {{ill|Muraji|en|Muraji|qid=Q2735611|lt=Murai}} appears, suggesting the existence of officials responsible for managing the Himuro for the Imperial Court. For example, in the {{ill|Kamo clan|fr|Clan Kamo|ja|賀茂県主氏|pt|Clã Kamo|qid=Q2975287|lt=Kamo clan}}—a family that produced priests for {{ill|Kamo shrines|cs|Svatyně Kamo|de|Kamo-Schrein|fa|معابد کامو|fi|Kamo-jinja|fr|Sanctuaires Kamo|id|Kuil Kamo|it|Santuario di Kamo|ja|賀茂神社|my|ခမိုနတ်ကျောင်း|pt|Santuário Kamo|ru|Камо-дзиндзя|simple|Kamo Shrine|th|ศาลเจ้าคาโมะ|uk|Святилище Камо|vi|Đền thờ Kamo|zh|賀茂神社|qid=Q1306606|lt=Kamo Shrine}}—genealogical records mention "Himuro" and the "Murai" surname.

Under the {{ill|Ritsuryō|en|Ritsuryō|qid=Q742460|lt=Ritsuryō system}}, Himuro and ice production officials belonged to the {{ill|Main Water Office|ja|主水司|qid=Q11368771}} of the {{ill|Ministry of the Imperial Household|en|Ministry of the Imperial Household|qid=Q8193428|lt=Ministry of the Imperial Household}}. The role of managing Himuro continued in various forms throughout history but disappeared during the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|qid=Q3125096|lt=Meiji period}}.

In the {{ill|Hokuriku region|en|Hokuriku region|qid=Q381025|lt=Hokuriku region}}, from the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|qid=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}, there was a custom of presenting Himuro ice to the shogunate on {{ill|June 1 (Lunisolar)|cdo|6 nguŏk 1 hô̤ (nùng-lĭk)|ja|6月1日 (旧暦)|ko|음력 6월 1일|zh|六月初一|zh_min_nan|6 goe̍h 1 ji̍t (kū-le̍k)|zh_yue|六月初一|qid=Q839637}} each year. However, with the Meiji period, natural ice became commercially available, and demand for refrigeration grew through the {{ill|Taishō era|ja|大正時代|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Taishō period|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大正|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q329174}}, leading to the construction of new snow storage facilities. Conversely, from the 1890s onward, mechanical ice began replacing natural ice, and freezing facilities were developed. By the early {{ill|Shōwa era|ja|昭和時代|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōwa period|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 昭和|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q327567}}, snow storage facilities were gradually phased out. After World War II, stricter regulations under the {{ill|Food Sanitation Act|ja|食品衛生法|qid=Q11666046}} and the widespread adoption of electric refrigerators in the 1960s led to the near-total disappearance of snow storage facilities by around 1962.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Ikegami|first=Yoshiyori|date=1999-04-28|title=The Distribution and Rise and Fall of Snow Storage Facilities in Hokuriku|url=https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/chirikagaku/54/2/54_KJ00003720149/_article/-char/ja/|journal=Geographical Science|volume=54|issue=2|pages=126, 129-134|publisher=Geographical Science Society|doi=10.20630/chirikagaku.54.2_126}}</ref>

There is also a {{ill|Noh|en|Noh|qid=Q226887|lt=Noh play}} with Himuro as its subject, classified as an aragami-mono (荒神物) play.

=== Himuro in the Engishiki ===

In {{ill|831|en|831|qid=Q30372|lt=831}} (Tenchō 8), three additional Himuro were established in both Yamashiro and Kawachi provinces.<ref name="kokushi"/><ref>"Nihon Kōki" fragments (found in "Nihon Kiraku"), entry dated August 20, 831.</ref>

=== Shrines Dedicated to Himuro ===

In {{ill|Heijō-kyō|en|Heijō-kyō|qid=Q862509|lt=Heijō-kyō}}, a Himuro was placed on {{ill|Kasugayama|ja|春日山|zh|春日山|qid=Q11513600|lt=Mount Kasuga}} for imperial ice offerings. After the capital moved to {{ill|Heian-kyō|en|Heian-kyō|qid=Q751907|lt=Heian-kyō}}, the {{ill|Himuro Shrine|en|Himuro Shrine|qid=Q11549570|lt=Himuro Shrine}} was established in {{ill|Kasugano, Nara City|ja|春日野町|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasugano, Nara City|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q18988212}}, enshrining the Himuro from Nara.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Himuro Shrine|url=http://www.himurojinja.jp|publisher=Himuro Shrine Official Website|accessdate=2012-05-21}}</ref> It is also known as {{ill|Himuro Gongen|ja|氷室権現}}.

=== Place Names ===

Himuro often remains as a place name where it once existed. Examples include "Himuro-cho" in {{ill|Nishigamo, Kyoto|ja|西賀茂氷室町}}, Kyoto, and "Himuro" in {{ill|Kamikawa, Izumo City|ja|神氷氷室}}, {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|en|Shimane Prefecture|qid=Q132751|lt=Shimane Prefecture}}. There are also numerous settlements across Japan named {{ill|Himuro Village|ja|氷室村|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Himuro Village|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11549564}} and {{ill|himurochou|ja|氷室町|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Himuro Town|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q18989720}}.

Additionally, names like {{ill|Mount Himuro|ja|氷室山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Himuro|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135578952}}, {{ill|Mount Himuro|ja|氷室岳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Himuro-dake|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11549563}}, Himuro Plateau, Himuro River, Himuro Valley, {{ill|Himuro Falls|ja|氷室大滝|qid=Q140446095}}, Himuro Pond, and Himuro Wakare (an intersection or junction) can also be found.

== Traditional Events ==

On the last Sunday of {{ill|January|en|January|qid=Q108|lt=January}}, snow is packed into the Himuro hut (氷室の仕込み), and on {{ill|June 30|en|June 30|qid=Q2657|lt=June 30}}, the snow is taken out, an event called "Himuro Opening" (氷室開き). In the heavy snowfall region of {{ill|Ishikawa Prefecture|en|Ishikawa Prefecture|qid=Q131281|lt=Ishikawa Prefecture}} and {{ill|Kanazawa|en|Kanazawa|qid=Q191130|lt=Kanazawa City}} and its surroundings, there used to be many Himuro sites. Ice was a valuable commodity for common people during the summer, and a custom emerged to eat {{ill|Himuro Manju|ja|氷室饅頭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Himuro Manju|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11549574}}, said to resemble ice, on {{ill|July 1|en|July 1|qid=Q2700|lt=July 1}} to pray for {{ill|Health|en|Health|qid=Q12147|lt=health}}, a tradition that continues today. The Himuro Opening event ceased in the {{ill|1950s|ja|昭和30th year 代}} (around {{ill|1955|en|1955|qid=Q18577|lt=1955}}-{{ill|1965|en|1965|qid=Q2650|lt=1965}}) but was revived in {{ill|1986|en|1986|qid=Q2430|lt=1986}} (Showa 61). However, in recent years, continuous warm winters have led to snow shortages, and the event was once threatened when the {{ill|Hakuenro Hotel|ja|白雲楼ホテル|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hakuenro Hotel|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11580438}}, which owned the Himuro hut at {{ill|Yuwaku Onsen|en|Yuwaku Onsen|qid=Q11563731|lt=Yuwaku Onsen}}, went bankrupt in {{ill|1998|en|1998|qid=Q2089|lt=1998}} (Heisei 10). Thanks to the permission of the bankruptcy trustee, the Himuro event near {{ill|Lake Gyokusen|ja|玉泉湖|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gyokusen Lake|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11572696}} continues today, with ice presented to local areas (Ishikawa Prefecture and Kanazawa City) as well as {{ill|Itabashi|en|Itabashi|qid=Q232635|lt=Itabashi Ward}} and {{ill|Meguro|en|Meguro|qid=Q233903|lt=Meguro Ward}} in Tokyo, which have historical ties to the {{ill|Maeda clan|en|Maeda clan|qid=Q578033|lt=Maeda clan}}.<ref>[http://yuwaku.gr.jp/himuro/ Himuro] Yuwaku Tourism Association (Accessed July 10, 2018)</ref><ref>[https://www.city.meguro.tokyo.jp/smph/gyosei/koho/hodo_news/20180704.html "Himuro Snow and Ice" Arrives at Meguro Ward Office - A Cool Gift from Kanazawa Yuwaku Onsen (July 4, 2018)] Meguro Ward (Accessed July 10, 2018)</ref>

In {{ill|Yatsushiro|en|Yatsushiro|qid=Q734479|lt=Yatsushiro City}}, {{ill|Kumamoto Prefecture|en|Kumamoto Prefecture|qid=Q130308|lt=Kumamoto Prefecture}}, the {{ill|Himuro Festival|ja|氷室祭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Himuro Festival|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135578957}} is held at {{ill|Yatsushiro Shrine|ja|八代神社}} (also known as {{ill|Myōken Shrine|ja|妙見宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Myoken Shrine|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 妙見宮 (曖昧さ回避)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q16767999}}) from {{ill|May 31|en|May 31|qid=Q2591|lt=May 31}} to {{ill|June 1|en|June 1|qid=Q2625|lt=June 1}}.<ref name="KumamotoPublicRelations">{{Cite web|title=Himuro Festival Specialty Yukimochi - Kumamoto's Culinary Traditions |url=http://www.kininaru-k.jp/2008/back_doc/05/0529/syoku.html |work=Kumamoto Public Relations (Official Website) |publisher=Kumamoto Prefecture PR Office, Colors Planning Co., Ltd. |accessdate=2012-05-21}}</ref> This festival day is colloquially known as "Kootsuitachi" (氷朔日), and it is customary to eat {{ill|Yukimochi|ja|雪餅}}, rice cakes made by kneading {{ill|Rice flour|en|Rice flour|qid=Q1269205|lt=rice flour}} with water and steaming them in a {{ill|Bamboo steamer|en|Bamboo steamer|qid=Q3267901|lt=seiro (steamer)}}, resembling snow clumps.<ref name="KumamotoPublicRelations" />

In {{ill|Nikkō|en|Nikkō|qid=Q235753|lt=Nikkō City}}, {{ill|Tochigi Prefecture|en|Tochigi Prefecture|qid=Q44843|lt=Tochigi Prefecture}}, there used to be about ten natural ice producers. Today, only three remain:<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.shimotsuke.co.jp/dosoon/official/20120105/693564|title=Shimotsuke Newspaper Video News DoSOON - Natural Ice Harvest Begins in Nikko|accessdate=2012-08-25}}</ref> the fourth-generation {{ill|Ice Maker Tokujirō|ja|氷屋徳次郎}} ({{ill|Yoshishin Himuro|ja|吉新氷室|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshishin Himuro|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135578959}})<ref>[http://www.chirorin.com/buy_ice.html Natural Ice | Official Website of Chirorin Village, Nikko Kirifuri Highlands]</ref><ref>[http://foodpianikko.jp/SHOP/nni10.html Nikko Natural Ice by the Fourth Generation Tokujirō]</ref>, {{ill|Shogetsu Himuro|ja|松月氷室|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shogetsu Himuro|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135578962}}<ref>[https://ameblo.jp/shogetsu-goodjob/entry-11059313541.html A Detailed Story About Natural Ice]</ref><ref>[https://ameblo.jp/shogetsu-goodjob/entry-10926137751.html Do You Know About "Natural Ice"?]</ref>, and {{ill|Mitsuboshi Himuro|ja|三ツ星氷室|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mitsuboshi Himuro|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=Q135578965}}, all of which store and sell natural ice.
